questiontext.text:
Goal

Write a subclass that chains to its base, plus two functions that expose a missing chain and a class's resolution order.

How this works in Python

Java extends a class with a keyword, and it writes one line of your constructor for you without telling you.

public class Sensor {
    protected final String name;
    protected final List<Double> readings = new ArrayList<>();

    public Sensor(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    public String describe() {
        return name + " holds " + readings.size() + " readings";
    }
}

public class PressureSensor extends Sensor {
    private final String unit;

    public PressureSensor(String name, String unit) {
        super(name);
        this.unit = unit;
    }

    @Override
    public String describe() {
        return super.describe() + " in " + unit;
    }
}

Here is the same pair in Python.

class PressureSensor(Sensor):
    def __init__(self, name: str, unit: str) -> None:
        super().__init__(name)
        self.unit = unit

    def describe(self) -> str:
        return f"{super().describe()} in {self.unit}"

Four things changed, and one of them will bite you this week.

The parent goes in parentheses

There is no extends keyword and no implements. Write the parent's name in brackets after the child's name and the subclass exists.

Python does not chain constructors

This is the one that bites. Leave super(name) out of a Java constructor and javac inserts a call to the no-argument parent constructor for you, or refuses to compile when there is not one. Python inserts nothing at all. A subclass __init__ that forgets super().__init__(name) is legal Python, runs without a murmur, and hands back an object where self.name and self.readings were never created.

Nothing raises at the point of the mistake. The object gets built, returned and passed around. The first method that reaches for a missing attribute raises AttributeError, and by then you are a long way from the constructor that caused it.

Overriding needs no keyword

Define a method in the subclass with the same name as one in the parent and yours wins. Nothing like @Override holds you to the spelling, so a typo quietly makes a new method instead, and the parent's version keeps running for the rest of the program. A later tier of this topic adds the marker that makes that promise checkable.

super() takes brackets

Java writes super.describe(). Python writes super().describe(), because super() is a call that hands back a proxy object standing in for the parent. Inside a class body Python works out the arguments that call needs, so you type the empty brackets and nothing else.

Call the parent's version rather than copying what it returns. super().describe() still tells the truth after somebody edits the parent, and a copied sentence goes stale in silence.

Last, the part Java has not got. A Python class may list more than one parent.

class LoggedAlarmSensor(Sensor, Logged, Alarmed):
    pass

Two parents can define the same method, so Python needs a rule for which one wins. The rule produces the method resolution order, written MRO, which is the list of classes Python walks through when it looks a name up. Every class carries its own list as __mro__, and that list runs broadly left to right across the parents you wrote. It finishes at object, because every class in Python inherits from object in the end.

Recognise multiple inheritance when you read it. Do not reach for it yet.

Your task

The answer box holds Sensor and four more classes. Leave all five exactly as they are, including the broken one. Write these three.

  • PressureSensor, a subclass of Sensor, taking name and unit. Chain to the base with super().__init__(name), then store unit. Override describe to return f"{super().describe()} in {unit}". Write no add method, because the inherited one already works.
  • forgot_super() builds ForgetfulSensor("p1", "bar"), calls describe() on it inside a try, catches the AttributeError, and returns f"AttributeError: {..}" with the message text in the slot.
  • mro_names(target) returns the __name__ of every class in target.__mro__, in order.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Call super().__init__(name). Python chains nothing for you, and that is the line Java was writing behind your back.
  • Do not assign self.name, and do not go near readings. The base owns both, and a copy of its work is a copy that drifts.
  • Build describe on top of super().describe(). Retyping the base sentence makes it stale the day somebody edits the parent.
  • Reach the parent through super(). Writing Sensor.describe(self) works today and breaks the day the hierarchy moves.
  • Do not edit the supplied block. ForgetfulSensor stays broken, because it is the exhibit.
  • Annotate every signature. __init__ gets -> None, and self never gets an annotation.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

testcode.text: inlet = PressureSensor("inlet", "bar") inlet.add(1.5) inlet.add(2.5) print(inlet.name, inlet.unit) print(inlet.readings) print(inlet.describe())

expected.text: inlet bar [1.5, 2.5] inlet holds 2 readings in bar
AttributeError: 'ForgetfulSensor' object has no attribute 'name' ['PressureSensor', 'Sensor', 'object'] ['LoggedAlarmSensor', 'Sensor', 'Logged', 'Alarmed', 'object'] logged

testcode.text: import inspect src = inspect.getsource(PressureSensor) assert "super().__init__" in src, "rule broken: chain to the base initialiser" assert "super().describe()" in src, "rule broken: build on the base description" assert "self.name" not in src, "rule broken: let super().__init__ set the name" assert "readings" not in src, "rule broken: the base owns readings" assert "def add" not in src, "rule broken: the inherited add already works" assert "Sensor." not in src, "rule broken: reach the parent through super()" first = PressureSensor("first", "bar") second = PressureSensor("second", "psi") first.add(9.0) first.add(3.0) print(first.describe()) print(second.describe()) print(first.readings is second.readings)

expected.text: first holds 2 readings in bar second holds 0 readings in psi False

questiontext.text:
Goal

Fill the abstract holes in a supplied safety-check base class with two concrete checks, a custom exception and one demonstration function.

How this works in Python

In Java you write abstract class or interface, then extends or implements, and the compiler stops you the moment a method is missing. Python has none of those keywords. A base class goes in parentheses after the class name, and nothing is checked until the program runs.

class RangeCheck(SafetyCheck):
    ...

The three dots are the Ellipsis literal. Python needs a statement inside every body, and the dots are a statement, so they stand in for code you have not written. pass from the classes topic does the same job.

Without help, that base would be a suggestion. A subclass could skip a method and Python would only complain at the call. The abstract base class closes the gap.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class SafetyCheck(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def evaluate(self, reading: float) -> bool:
        """Return True when the reading is acceptable."""

Inheriting from ABC and marking a method with @abstractmethod makes Python refuse to build the object. Call SafetyCheck("base") and you get TypeError before a single line of your code runs. A subclass that implements every abstract method builds normally.

The triple-quoted string under evaluate is a docstring. Python needs a statement in a body, and a docstring is a statement, so an abstract method needs nothing else.

Carry your Java habits into this exercise and three more differences catch you.

No constructor chaining

Java inserts super() for you when you leave it out. Python never does. Write a subclass __init__ that forgets super().__init__(name) and the base's attributes never exist. No compiler stops you. You find out when a method reaches for self.failures and gets AttributeError.

def __init__(self, name: str, low: float, high: float) -> None:
    super().__init__(name)
    self.low = low
    self.high = high

Nothing is final

Every method can be overridden. That makes the template method pattern plain. The base writes a concrete run() that calls the abstract hooks, and a subclass fills the holes. Some hooks are abstract and force you to write them. Others are concrete and give you a default you can replace, and failure_error below is one of those.

A custom exception is a subclass and nothing more

No checked exceptions, no throws clause, no fields required.

class OutOfRange(CheckFailed):
    """Raised when a reading sits outside the allowed band."""

Catch the parent and you catch the child, so except CheckFailed still catches an OutOfRange.

Last, the reason Python can live without interfaces. Look at the consumer supplied in the answer box.

def report(checks: Iterable[SafetyCheck]) -> str:
    return " | ".join(check.describe() for check in checks)

The annotation is a note to a reader and to a type checker, and at run time it stops nothing. This function tests no type and calls no isinstance. It calls describe() and that is the entire contract. Any object with that method is accepted. This is called duck typing, and it is why a Python consumer needs no interface to program against.

Your task

The answer box holds CheckFailed, SafetyCheck and report already written. Leave all three exactly as they are. The base sets self.name and self.failures, and its run(reading) returns f"{name} accepted {reading}" on success, or records the reading and raises self.failure_error(reading) on failure. Write the rest.

  • OutOfRange, a subclass of CheckFailed.
  • RangeCheck(name, low, high). evaluate accepts a reading from low to high inclusive. describe returns f"{name} keeps readings in {low}..{high}". Override failure_error to return OutOfRange(f"{name} rejected {reading} outside {low}..{high}").
  • RateOfChangeCheck(name, limit) holds the previous reading, starting at None. The first reading is always accepted and becomes the previous one. A later reading is accepted when its distance from the previous reading is limit or less. Store a later reading as the previous one either way. describe returns f"{name} allows jumps up to {limit}". Leave failure_error alone here, so this check raises the plain CheckFailed.
  • abstract_error() tries to build SafetyCheck("base") and catches the TypeError. Return f"TypeError and the word abstract appears: {..}". The slot holds whether "abstract" appears in the message text.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Do not edit SafetyCheck, CheckFailed or report. The tests use them exactly as given.
  • Do not write your own run. The base already wrote it, and you are filling the abstract holes.
  • Call super().__init__(..) in both subclasses. Python does not chain constructors for you.
  • Assign nothing in a class body. Every attribute is born in __init__.
  • Do not write isinstance anywhere in your answer.
  • Do not register your classes with anything. Matching the shape is the whole interface.
  • Annotate every signature, the abstract ones included. A hole in a base class still has a shape, so say what it is.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

testcode.text: band = RangeCheck("band", 0, 100) print(band.run(50)) try: band.run(140) except CheckFailed as problem: print(type(problem).__name__, "->", problem) print(band.failures) print(band.describe())

expected.text: band accepted 50 OutOfRange -> band rejected 140 outside 0..100 [140] band keeps readings in 0..100

testcode.text: rate = RateOfChangeCheck("rate", 5) print(rate.run(10)) print(rate.run(13)) try: rate.run(40) except CheckFailed as problem: print(type(problem).__name__, "->", problem) print(rate.failures) print(report([RangeCheck("band", 0, 100), rate])) print(abstract_error())

expected.text: rate accepted 10 rate accepted 13 CheckFailed -> rate rejected 40 [40] band keeps readings in 0..100 | rate allows jumps up to 5 TypeError and the word abstract appears: True

testcode.text: import inspect src = inspect.getsource(RangeCheck) + inspect.getsource(RateOfChangeCheck) assert src.count("super().__init__") == 2, "rule broken: call super().__init__ in both classes" assert "def run" not in src, "rule broken: do not re-implement run" assert "isinstance" not in src, "rule broken: no isinstance" assert "isinstance" not in inspect.getsource(report), "rule broken: report must stay duck typed" assert issubclass(OutOfRange, CheckFailed), "rule broken: OutOfRange must subclass CheckFailed" first = RangeCheck("first", 0, 10) second = RangeCheck("second", 0, 10) try: first.run(99) except CheckFailed: pass print(first.failures, second.failures, first.failures is second.failures) print(report([first]))

questiontext.text:
Goal

Repair two silent override typos in a four-class hierarchy and give every method that hands back an instance the right return type.

How this works in Python

Java has @Override. Misspell the method name and javac stops the build, because the annotation promises a base method with that exact signature exists.

class TemperatureSensor extends Sensor {
    @Override
    String describ() { return "temperature " + name; }   // does not compile
}

Python 3.12 added the same marker as typing.override. It is checked by a type checker and not at run time, which is the enforcement lesson from the type hints topic again. Its only run-time act is to set __override__ to True on the function, so a tool can find it later.

from typing import override


class PressureSensor(Sensor):
    @override
    def describe(self) -> str:
        return f"pressure {self.name}"

Without the marker a misspelling costs you the override in silence. def describ in a subclass is a valid new method, so Python defines it, keeps the inherited describe, and runs the base version for the rest of the program. Nothing raises. The subclass looks specialised and behaves like its parent, and the only symptom is a log line that says the wrong thing.

typing.Self arrived in 3.11 and answers a different question. A method that returns its own instance has a return type that depends on the class it was called on, and naming the class in the annotation freezes that answer at the base.

class Sensor:
    def calibrate(self, offset: float) -> "Sensor":     # the lie
        return type(self)(self.name, self.value + offset)

PressureSensor("p1", 1.0).calibrate(0.5) hands back a PressureSensor at run time, because type(self) asks the instance what it is. The annotation still claims Sensor, so the type checker forgets the subclass and rejects the next .bar_reading() call. Write -> Self and the annotation tracks whatever class the method was reached through.

The same applies to an alternative constructor, which is a classmethod that builds an instance from something other than the usual arguments. It receives the class as cls, so cls(...) already builds the right subclass. Annotate it -> Self and the two halves agree.

@classmethod
def from_text(cls, text: str) -> Self:
    name, _, raw = text.partition("=")
    return cls(name, float(raw))
Your task

The answer box holds a four-class hierarchy with two subtle defects in it. Two subclasses each carry a method whose name is one character short of the base method it meant to override. Both classes therefore inherit the base behaviour and nobody is told.

Repair the hierarchy.

  • Fix both misspellings so each subclass overrides the method it was aiming at.
  • Put @override on all three genuine overrides.
  • Give calibrate and from_text the return type Self, in Sensor and in RelaySensor.
  • Leave every method body as it stands. PressureSensor reports f"pressure {self.name} at {self.value:.1f} bar", TemperatureSensor reports f"temperature {self.name} at {self.value:.1f} C", and RelaySensor doubles the offset it is given.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Put @override on every method that overrides one. A type checker confirms the promise, and Python never will.
  • Write -> Self. Naming the class in the return type becomes a lie the moment somebody subclasses it.
  • Build the new instance through type(self) or cls. A hard-coded Sensor(...) hands a subclass back the wrong type.
  • Fix the typo in the subclass. Renaming the base method to match the typo makes the tests pass and the design worse.
  • Annotate every signature. Parameters and return type, no exceptions.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

testcode.text: sensors = [Sensor("s0", 1.0), PressureSensor("p1", 12.34), TemperatureSensor("t1", 68.55), RelaySensor("r1", 3.0)] for sensor in sensors: print(sensor.describe()) print(hasattr(TemperatureSensor, "describ"), hasattr(RelaySensor, "calibrat"))

expected.text: s0=1.0 pressure p1 at 12.3 bar temperature t1 at 68.5 C r1=3.0 False False

testcode.text: warm = TemperatureSensor("t1", 68.5).calibrate(1.5) print(type(warm).__name__, warm.describe()) relay = RelaySensor("r1", 3.0).calibrate(1.5) print(type(relay).__name__, relay.describe()) built = PressureSensor.from_text("p9=12.5") print(type(built).__name__, built.describe()) print(type(Sensor.from_text("s9=1.5")).__name__)

expected.text: TemperatureSensor temperature t1 at 70.0 C RelaySensor r1=6.0 PressureSensor pressure p9 at 12.5 bar Sensor
nothing in Sensor is named this True True True True

testcode.text:
import inspect
for cls, gone in ((TemperatureSensor, "describ"), (RelaySensor, "calibrat")): assert gone not in vars(cls), "rule broken: fix the spelling, do not keep the stray method" assert "describe" in vars(Sensor), "rule broken: leave the base method name alone" assert "calibrate" in vars(Sensor), "rule broken: leave the base method name alone" for cls, method in ((PressureSensor, "describe"), (TemperatureSensor, "describe"), (RelaySensor, "calibrate")): marked = getattr(vars(cls)[method], "__override__", False) assert marked is True, "rule broken: mark every genuine override with @override" for func in (Sensor.calibrate, Sensor.from_text, RelaySensor.calibrate): assert func.__annotations__["return"] is Self, "rule broken: return Self, not the class name" for func in (Sensor.calibrate, Sensor.from_text.__func__): assert "Sensor(" not in inspect.getsource(func), "rule broken: build through type(self) or cls"
print(Sensor.from_text("s1=2.5").describe()) print(type(TemperatureSensor.from_text("t9=70.0").calibrate(0.5)).__name__) print(sorted(name for name in vars(RelaySensor) if not name.startswith("__")))
